title: I'm building a GBA game with AI agents: prototyped in Godot, running on a real Game Boy Advance
author: Tri8ar
selftext:
Hey. I'm working on 2ND HEARTBEAT, a small retro space story about trust, and

the target is the Game Boy Advance. Not a GBA-styled game: an actual ROM.



The first half of the clip is that ROM running in mGBA: a raid, the return to

base, and the debrief with your partner. The photos are the same build on my

AGS-101. The second half is the Godot prototype, the parts that haven't made

the jump to hardware yet.



Since this sub is about the how, here's the loop.



Godot is my design lab. A coding agent is hooked into the editor through MCP,

so an idea gets tried in minutes rather than evenings. But the prototypes are

held to the GBA spec from the start: 240×160, real sprite and palette budgets,

layers planned the way the hardware would draw them. Once something works

there, it moves to the GBA as a spike: a small Butano/C++ ROM that answers one

hardware question, like whether the debrief portrait fits the palette budget,

or whether a corridor can rush toward the camera by palette cycling alone.

What you see in the clip is about a month and a half of that.



That strict planning paid off more than I expected. Seeing the game on a real

GBA looking the way it does in Godot was a genuine shock: almost nothing lost

in the port, and in places it even looks better, thanks to crisp pixels on the

native screen and a perfectly even refresh rate.



AI does a lot of the work here. All of the code is written by agents, on both

sides. The art goes through AI too: some of it is generated, some of it is

refine passes over my own drawings and sketches, and most of it gets cleaned

up by hand in Aseprite to fit GBA palettes. I make the calls, review what goes in, and an iteration

only counts once I've played it myself, ideally on the handheld. No intent to

pass any of it off as something it isn't.



One piece I'm happy with: the choice drum from the debrief. In Godot it's

ordinary tweened UI. On the GBA, the scaling runs on the hardware's OBJ affine

units and the transparency is per-scanline blending. No software rendering at

all, on a machine from 2001.



And one lesson. Agents love building ever more elaborate test harnesses:

frame-by-frame autopilots, capture rigs, the works. At some point verification

turned into a project of its own. So now there's a written rule in the repo:

if checking something becomes a fight, the agent stops and asks me to just

play it. My thumb on the D-pad is the cheapest test I have.



There's no audio yet, and plenty of rough edges. But the loop works.



Is anyone else here targeting real retro hardware with agents? I'm curious

what your verification loop looks like.
